blocks.text: Protect the main thread, object-URL lifecycle, transfer recovery, and accessible feedback without weakening the upload state machine.

Even a single-image upload can be expensive: decoding, resizing, and uploading large files can jank the UI. Keep image work off the main thread when possible, throttle progress updates, and make retries safe.

Upload performance and recovery evidence:
- Awareness of image decoding/resizing cost and main-thread impact.
- Stable progress + retry behavior on flaky networks.
- Memory hygiene (object URLs, avoiding base64 blobs).
- A path to extend to multi-image or chunked uploads.

blocks.title: Performance & memory hygiene
items: Use createImageBitmap + OffscreenCanvas or a Web Worker for resize/compress.
Throttle progress updates (e.g., 100-200ms) to avoid re-render storms.
Avoid base64 in state; keep File + object URL only.
Use AbortController to cancel in-flight uploads on replace/remove.
Cap memory usage if multiple previews are added later.

blocks.title: UX & accessibility polish
items: Ensure the main control is a clear, focusable target (button or label-wrap around file input) with descriptive text.
Display error messages in a region with role="alert" or wired via aria-describedby so screen readers announce them immediately.
Use distinct visual cues for idle, validating, uploading, finalizing, complete, cancelled, and error, not just color changes.
Make sure "Replace" and "Remove" are reachable by keyboard and have clear labels (not just icons).
On error, keep focus in a sensible place (e.g. on the control or on the first action), so the user can fix the problem quickly.
On mobile, avoid cramped layouts: give enough padding around the button, preview, and actions so taps are reliable.

blocks.title: Upload performance and recovery trade-offs
rows: Use createImageBitmap or a worker + OffscreenCanvas for preprocessing.
Uploads fail mid-flight; users lose progress.
Retry with backoff, allow cancel, and resume if the backend supports chunking.
Reduce every byte update, then coalesce visible progress paints only when profiling shows they are too frequent.
Multiple previews leak memory over time.
Revoke URLs on replace/remove/unmount and avoid base64.
Use a vertical layout and limit preview size with object-fit.

steps.title: 1. Start upload with AbortController
steps.text: Create an AbortController per attempt in a runtime registry or ref, not serializable state. Store only attempt identity and status, then expose Cancel.

steps.title: 2. Handle cancel
steps.text: On cancel/replace, call controller.abort(), reset progress, and revoke preview URLs.

steps.title: 3. Retry with backoff
steps.text: On failure, show Retry and attempt again with exponential backoff.

steps.title: 4. Throttle progress UI
steps.text: Preserve the latest byte count and coalesce only visible progress paints when measured rendering cost justifies it.

items.label: Key UX lever
items.helperText: Users trust the upload if they can see and recover.

blocks.title: Upload recovery invariant
blocks.text: The deep dive is about performance and reliability: keep image work off the main thread, throttle progress updates, and make retry/cancel safe.

blocks.title: Failure modes
rows: Revoke on replace, remove, and unmount.
Request a new session for the same active attempt.
The preview and user intent remain.
The UI does not invent a percentage.
Retry with the same idempotency key.

blocks.text: Use a visible label and native file input, with drag and drop as an enhancement rather than the only path. Error text is associated with the input, replacement and removal are real buttons, progress has a readable status, and preview alternative text describes its purpose without repeating adjacent labels. Focus stays on the triggering control after recovery.

Test large files, corrupt images, EXIF orientation, unsupported formats, memory pressure, aborted preprocessing, expired sessions, lost finalization responses, replacement races, reduced motion, and mobile capture. Track preview time, upload completion, cancellation, retry, memory, and error correction.

blocks.title: image upload preview answer rubric
items: Must — Model the eight upload state fields and guard every callback with the active attempt identity.
Must — Revoke object URLs and abort transfer work on replace, remove, and unmount.
Strong signal — Separate local validation, upload-session creation, transfer, and authoritative finalization.
Strong signal — Report real byte progress when available and keep unknown progress indeterminate.
Expert stretch — Move measured image preprocessing off the main thread and bound memory across files.
Red flag — Storing base64 previews indefinitely or allowing a stale upload callback to replace a newer file.
